stem: The Earth, the Moon and the Sun are all part of the __________.
solution: The Sun, the planets including Earth, and their moons together make up the Solar System.

stem: The Sun is a __________.
solution: The Sun is a star — a huge, hot ball of glowing gases at the centre of the Solar System.

stem: The Earth's natural satellite is the __________.
solution: The Moon is the only natural satellite of the Earth.

stem: The spinning of the Earth about its own axis is called __________.
solution: Rotation is the spinning of the Earth on its axis, which causes day and night.

stem: The Earth completes one rotation about its axis in about __________.
solution: The Earth takes about 24 hours to complete one rotation, giving us a day and a night.

stem: Day and night are caused by the __________ of the Earth.
solution: As the Earth rotates, one half faces the Sun (day) while the other is in darkness (night).

stem: The movement of the Earth around the Sun is called __________.
solution: Revolution is the movement of the Earth in its orbit around the Sun.

stem: The Earth takes about __________ to complete one revolution around the Sun.
solution: One revolution of the Earth around the Sun takes about 365¼ days — one year.

stem: The imaginary line about which the Earth rotates is called its __________.
solution: The axis is the imaginary line through the poles about which the Earth spins.

stem: The Earth's axis is __________ with respect to its orbital plane.
solution: The Earth's axis is tilted (about 23.5°), which is responsible for the seasons.

stem: The main cause of the seasons on the Earth is the __________.
options: tilt of Earth's axis combined with its revolution
changing distance from the Sun only
solution: The tilt of the axis as the Earth revolves makes different regions receive different amounts of sunlight, causing seasons.

stem: The Moon takes about __________ to complete one revolution around the Earth.
solution: The Moon revolves around the Earth in roughly a month.

stem: The changing shapes of the bright part of the Moon seen from the Earth are called the __________.
solution: The phases of the Moon are the different lit shapes seen as the Moon revolves around the Earth.

stem: The Moon appears to shine because it __________.
solution: The Moon is non-luminous; we see it because it reflects light from the Sun.

stem: The phase in which the whole bright disc of the Moon is visible is called __________.
solution: At full moon the entire lit face of the Moon faces the Earth, so we see a full bright disc.

stem: The phase in which the Moon is not visible at all in the sky is called __________.
solution: At new moon the lit side faces away from Earth, so the Moon is not seen.

stem: The time between one full moon and the next is about __________.
solution: The cycle of Moon phases repeats in roughly a month (a lunar month).

stem: The surface of the Moon has craters mainly because of __________.
solution: Moon craters were formed by meteorite impacts; with no atmosphere they are preserved.

stem: The Moon has no atmosphere, so on the Moon there is __________.
solution: Lacking an atmosphere, the Moon has no air, no water, no weather and no sound.

stem: The same side of the Moon always faces the Earth because the Moon's rotation period equals its __________.
solution: The Moon rotates once per revolution, so the same face is always turned towards Earth.

stem: The pattern of stars that appears to form a recognisable shape in the sky is called a __________.
solution: A constellation is a group of stars that appears to form a pattern in the night sky.

stem: The star that appears almost fixed in the northern sky and helps find directions is the __________.
solution: The Pole Star stays nearly stationary above the north pole and is used to find the north direction.

stem: The constellation used to locate the Pole Star is the __________.
solution: The two 'pointer' stars of Ursa Major (Saptarshi) point towards the Pole Star.

stem: Orion (the Hunter), a prominent winter constellation, is also called __________ in some traditions.
solution: Orion is known as Mriga in Indian tradition and is a well-known winter constellation.

stem: Stars appear to twinkle because their light is disturbed while passing through the Earth's __________.
solution: The Earth's moving atmosphere bends starlight irregularly, making stars appear to twinkle.

stem: Planets generally do not twinkle like stars because they __________.
options: are much closer and appear as small discs
solution: Planets are near enough to appear as tiny discs, so their light averages out and does not twinkle.

stem: The apparent daily east-to-west movement of the Sun across the sky is actually due to the Earth's __________.
solution: The Earth rotates west to east, making the Sun and stars appear to move east to west.

stem: A solar eclipse occurs on a __________.
solution: A solar eclipse can occur only at new moon, when the Moon is between the Sun and Earth.

stem: A lunar eclipse occurs on a __________.
solution: A lunar eclipse can occur only at full moon, when Earth is between the Sun and Moon.

stem: The Sun is the primary source of __________ for life on the Earth.
solution: The Sun provides the light and heat energy essential for life and weather on Earth.

stem: Compared with the Earth, the Sun is __________.
solution: The Sun is enormously larger than the Earth; it only looks small because it is very far away.

stem: The Moon is much smaller than the Earth but appears almost the same size as the Sun in the sky because __________.
options: it is very much closer to us
it is actually the same size as the Sun
solution: The Moon looks big because it is very close, even though it is far smaller than the distant Sun.

stem: A celestial body that revolves around a planet is called a __________.
solution: A satellite is a body that revolves around a planet; the Moon is Earth's natural satellite.

stem: Objects like the International Space Station placed in orbit by humans are called __________ satellites.
solution: Artificial satellites are human-made objects put into orbit around the Earth.

stem: Which of the following is closest to the Earth?
solution: The Moon, as Earth's satellite, is the nearest major celestial body to the Earth.

stem: Because the Moon has weaker gravity than the Earth, an object on the Moon would weigh __________.
solution: The Moon's gravity is about one-sixth of Earth's, so objects weigh less there.

stem: During the waxing phase, the bright portion of the Moon appears to be __________.
solution: During waxing, the lit part of the Moon grows larger each night up to full moon.

stem: During the waning phase, the bright part of the Moon appears to be __________.
solution: During waning, the lit part of the Moon shrinks each night after full moon towards new moon.

stem: The distances between celestial bodies in space are so large that they are measured in __________.
solution: A light year, the distance light travels in a year, is used for the vast distances between stars.

stem: One light year is the distance travelled by __________ in one year.
solution: A light year is the distance light travels in one year — a very large distance.

stem: Stars appear as tiny points of light mainly because they are __________.
solution: Stars look like points because they are at enormous distances from the Earth.

stem: A shooting star seen streaking across the night sky is actually a __________ burning up in the atmosphere.
solution: A meteor (shooting star) is a small space rock that glows as it burns in Earth's atmosphere.

stem: A meteor that survives its fall and reaches the Earth's surface is called a __________.
solution: A meteorite is the remnant of a meteor that lands on the Earth's surface.

stem: The tail of a comet always points __________ the Sun.
solution: A comet's tail is pushed by the solar wind and radiation, so it points away from the Sun.

stem: The band of countless stars visible as a faint milky streak across a dark sky is called the __________.
solution: The Milky Way is our galaxy, seen as a hazy band of stars across the night sky.

stem: The reason we do not feel the very high speed of the Earth's motion is that __________.
options: everything around us moves along with the Earth
solution: We move with the Earth and its atmosphere uniformly, so its motion is not felt.

stem: Sunrise and sunset happen at different times in different places because the Earth is __________ and rotating.
solution: On a rotating spherical Earth, different longitudes face the Sun at different times.

stem: The apparent path of the Sun in the sky is __________ in summer than in winter for places away from the equator.
solution: In summer the Sun rises higher and stays longer in the sky, giving longer, warmer days.

stem: The Earth is best described as a __________.
solution: The Earth is a planet that revolves around the Sun and does not produce its own light.

stem: The correct order of the three bodies during a total solar eclipse is __________.
solution: In a solar eclipse the Moon lies directly between the Sun and the Earth.
